Orange Cat Project · Night Report

The Last Meter

First night of the fast system: it won the open patio, and lost the doorstep. One approach repelled, one sprint straight through the sounds and into the house.

Night of 2026-08-31 → 09-01 · patrol.log, two reaction videos, overnight scorecard

Everything fired on time, every gate held, and the score is a split. The new loop saw every approach on frames a third of a second old and had sound in the air ~4 s after first sight — twice. At 01:52 that was enough: the cat probed to the flap under fire, backed out, and left. At 01:58 it wasn't: already close when the drill landed, the cat chose to sprint forward — through the bark, through the flap — and ate for eleven minutes. The exit at 02:09 was correctly silent under the new no-exit-fires rule.

The tactical lesson of night one: sound now controls the open patio, but the last meter in front of the door belongs to the cat.

Engagement 1, 01:52 — the repel

Engagement 2, 01:58 — the breach

Same cat, same defense, opposite outcome — the difference was range. At 01:52 the drill caught it mid-patio with the whole patio between it and safety in either direction. At 01:58 it was already closing on the door when the sound landed, and the shortest path away from the noise was through the flap toward the food. Under fire, it did the arithmetic correctly.

The exit, 02:09 — silence, on purpose

No reaction video exists for the exit (captures only run on a fire, and this one was silent by design) — this clip is assembled from the 15 frames the motion event saved, ~10 real seconds played at 2 fps. No person is visible in any frame; the 02:09:21 person stand-down came 5 seconds after the last saved frame, from the live stream. Dima's Protect NVR has the true continuous footage if wanted.

Questions for Dave & Dima

  1. Was anyone outside at 02:09? The person gate stood down on 1 of 6 frames at 02:09:21, a minute after the cat's exit, with the patio empty by 02:10. If Dima was up (as on 08-29), fine; if not, YOLO hallucinated a person on the departing cat and the burst is worth an eyeball. It cost nothing tonight, but the person gate's false-positive rate matters for the water decision.
  2. Did anyone hear the sounds? Five sounds played across 01:52–01:59, all full-volume close-range ones. The quiet far-growl tier never triggered — both approaches were first seen already close. Worth knowing whether the current volume woke anyone before we consider raising anything.
  3. Close-range doctrine. When the cat is first seen already near the door, the ladder ran drill → bark and lost the race. Options: jump straight to the harshest pair (drill + cat-fight scream, no gaps); shorten escalation intervals from 2–3s to ~1s at close range; or accept that close-range approaches are unwinnable by sound. Which experiment do you want next?
  4. Label fix (small): when orange goes to zero and the last detection touched the flap zone, log "likely went inside" instead of "target gone", and mark the visit so the record is honest in real time. Cosmetic, but tonight it had me announcing a win that wasn't. Approve?
  5. The strategic one. Night one splits the evidence: sound wins mid-patio, loses the last meter. The remaining levers are the sound chain getting faster (N3, ~0.7s less latency — buys maybe one more body-length), the close-range doctrine above, or the water discussion the 08-28 review deferred (aimed across the approach, person-gate fixed — which it now is). How many more nights of sound-only data do you want before that conversation?

Recommendations from tonight's data

  1. 1 · Engage on the first glimpse (~4 seconds recoverable). The breach timeline: patio empty at 01:58:12, cat visible at the fence corner by :18, but the deterrent only engaged at :23 — five seconds spent re-confirming with a burst vote designed for the old slow patrol. At the new 0.33s cadence, two consecutive live-frame orange verdicts give the same false-positive protection in 0.7 s. Skip the burst re-vote when the last two live classifications agree; the far growl is then in the air while the cat is still six seconds from the door.
  2. 2 · Rapid ladder at close range. The cat entered 3 s after the drill, hearing only one follow-up. For engagements that open near the door: ~1 s escalation intervals and jump straight to the harshest pair (drill → cat-fight). Honestly a one-extra-sound experiment, not a fix.
  3. 3 · Shrink the new sound files — done — and optionally stage them on HA. The three new sounds were 1–1.6 MB WAVs; over the tunnel that could cost 1–3 s exactly at the moment of fire. They are now 200–350 KB MP3s (fetch risk gone). Staging them on Home Assistant itself (box below) saves a further ~0.3–0.5 s per sound.
  4. 4 · Lengthen the last meter — the non-software fix (Dima's call). Entry came ~3 s after the sound landed. Anything that forces the final approach into an arc — a planter or obstacle between the fence-corner line and the flap — adds the 2–3 s that converts breaches into repels at current latency. No code, no habituation, compounds with everything above.
  5. 5 · Close the evidence gaps. Tonight produced three: no video of the exit (fixed by silent reaction capture on exiting/in_flap), no saved frames from the 02:09:21 person stand-down (save the burst on that rare, safety-critical gate), and a "target gone" log line that actually meant "target indoors" (label it "likely went inside" when the last detection touched the flap zone).
  6. 6 · Two asks for Dima. Pull NVR footage 02:09:00–02:10:00 (settles whether the person frame was real), and say whether five sounds at 2 am were audible in the house — that calibrates how much louder or denser we can afford to get.
  7. 7 · Hold on water, but set the tripwire now. The record: four clean repels mid-patio, two losses within a body-length of the door. Items 1–4 attack exactly that last meter. Proposed threshold, decided while nobody is frustrated: if the cat gets inside on 2 of the next 5 armed nights despite these changes, the water build starts.

For Dima — staging the sounds on Home Assistant (optional, 5 minutes)

What it does: Home Assistant currently fetches each deterrent sound from Dave's machine over the tunnel at the moment of fire. Hosting the files on HA itself makes every fire ~0.3–0.5 s faster. Nothing else changes on your side — same sounds, same hours, same rules.

How:

1. Download the sound pack: ha-staging.zip (1.5 MB — 4 WAVs + 3 MP3s + README)
2. Unzip it so the files sit in /config/www/ocp/ on Home Assistant (File editor add-on, Samba, or Studio Code Server — create the www/ocp folders if they don't exist)
3. Tell Dave it's done — he flips one setting on his side and the switch takes effect at the next restart.

If /config/www is new on your install, HA needs one restart to start serving it; after that the files are reachable at http://homeassistant:8123/local/ocp/… with no authentication, which is fine — they're dog barks.
